creator_or_source: Jan Zawadzki (primary version, published via Towards Data Science / Medium). Note: multiple related AI Canvas variants exist — Agrawal/Gans/Goldfarb (2018, HBR/Prediction Machines), Kevin Dewalt (2017, Prolego), DAIN Studios (2023, GenAI-specific), and Kerzel's Enterprise AI Canvas (2020, academic). This entry focuses on Zawadzki's AI Project Canvas as the most widely referenced under this exact name.
scope: Single phase — Focuses on project scoping and value communication. Covers initial project definition and stakeholder alignment, not the full ML lifecycle (deployment, monitoring, retraining are out of scope).
key_components:
The AI Project Canvas is a one-page visual tool inspired by Alexander Osterwalder's Business Model Canvas (2008), adapted specifically for AI/ML projects. It organizes thinking into 9 blocks across 4 quadrants:

**Central Block — Value Proposition**
- The heart of the canvas. Answers: what value does this AI project add to the organization?
- Can be a new AI-powered product generating revenue, or an improvement to an existing process cutting costs
- Must be clearly articulated so that non-technical stakeholders understand the 'why'

**Left Side — Ingredients (Build)**
- **Data**: What data is available and what data is needed? Sources, formats, volumes, quality, accessibility, and data collection requirements
- **Skills**: What technical and domain skills are needed? ML engineering, data engineering, domain expertise, labeling capabilities
- **Output**: The key metric or deliverable the model produces — accuracy, F1-score, precision, recall, latency, or a business KPI like minutes-spent-using-the-service

**Right Side — Integration (Deploy)**
- **Integration**: How will the AI model be integrated into existing systems, infrastructure, and workflows? API, batch processing, embedded in an app, etc.
- **Customers**: Who are the end users? Internal users (analysts, operators) or external customers who will interact with the AI-powered feature
- **Stakeholders**: Who else has a vested interest? Legal, UX, management, external contractors, regulators, non-profit groups

**Bottom — Financing**
- **Cost**: What are the expected costs? Data scientist salaries, labeling services, cloud computing, data acquisition, maintenance
- **Revenue**: How will the project generate returns? SaaS licensing, new product feature, cost reduction from automation, innovation initiative

**Workflow Logic**: The canvas creates a circular dependency flow: costs fund data wrangling using key skills to produce a target output → this output proposes new value to the organization → the value is integrated into existing architecture while communicating with stakeholders → customers benefit, generating revenue that justifies the costs.

**Related Variants** (for context):
- *Agrawal/Gans/Goldfarb AI Canvas* (2018): 7 elements focused on decision-making — Prediction, Judgment, Action, Outcome, Input, Training Data, Feedback. More economics-oriented, derived from 'Prediction Machines' book.
- *Kevin Dewalt's AI Canvas* (2017): Enterprise-focused, splits into business issues (left) and technical feasibility (right). Includes unique blocks for Policy & Process, Transfer Learning, and Success Criteria.
- *Enterprise AI Canvas* (Kerzel, 2020): Academic two-part canvas — Part 1 covers business view and organizational aspects, Part 2 covers ML model and data specifics.
typical_use_case: A product manager or AI team lead needs to pitch a new AI project to senior leadership. They spend 20-30 minutes filling out the canvas to articulate: the business value (e.g., 'reduce customer churn by 15% via predictive modeling'), what data and skills are required, how the model will integrate with existing CRM systems, who the stakeholders and end-users are, and what the project will cost versus the expected ROI. The filled canvas becomes a one-page project brief that replaces a lengthy slide deck for the initial go/no-go decision.
deliverables: Filled one-page canvas (visual poster or document format). The canvas serves as a project brief, communication artifact, and alignment tool. No formal score or quantitative output — the deliverable is the structured thinking and shared understanding it produces.
genai_relevance: Low — The AI Project Canvas (2019) was designed for classical ML projects: prediction models, computer vision, NLP classification, etc. It does not address GenAI-specific concerns such as foundation model selection, prompt engineering, fine-tuning vs. RAG architecture, hallucination risks, token costs, or responsible use of generative outputs. The 'Output' block assumes a single measurable metric (accuracy, F1), which maps poorly to generative tasks where quality is multidimensional and harder to quantify. However, DAIN Studios released a dedicated 'Generative AI Use Case Canvas' in 2023 that fills this gap. The Zawadzki canvas's general structure (value proposition, data, skills, cost, integration) remains a useful starting point but needs significant adaptation for LLM/GenAI projects.
accessibility_for_non_engineers: High — The canvas is explicitly business-oriented, inspired by the Business Model Canvas that MBA students already know. It uses plain language (value proposition, customers, cost, revenue) rather than technical ML jargon. The 9 blocks are self-explanatory and the visual one-page format is intuitive. Business students with no technical background can fill it out by focusing on the business quadrants (value proposition, customers, stakeholders, cost, revenue) while collaborating with a technical partner on the ingredients blocks (data, skills, output). The circular flow logic makes the business case easy to follow.
time_to_apply: 20-30 minutes for a first draft. Can be used in a 60-90 minute team workshop for a more thorough version with discussion and iteration.
free_or_paid: Free — Published as an open Medium/Towards Data Science article. Canvas image freely downloadable. Miro templates available at no cost (miro.com/miroverse/ai-canvas/ and miro.com/templates/ai-product-canvas/). Can be recreated on any whiteboard tool.
adoption_level: Widely adopted — One of the most referenced AI project scoping tools in data science education and practice. Featured on ml-ops.org, Experfy, Syndicai, and numerous AI project management resources. The broader family of AI canvases (including Agrawal et al. and Dewalt variants) is used at business schools including Rotman School of Management (University of Toronto). However, it has not achieved the universal standard status of the original Business Model Canvas.
ai_project_stage: Ideation — Primarily designed for the very early stage of an AI project: scoping, communicating the idea, and getting stakeholder buy-in before significant technical investment. Can also support PoC planning by clarifying what data and skills are needed and how success will be measured.
relevance_for_entrepreneurs: Highly valuable for AI startup founders and intrapreneurs. Key benefits: (1) Forces founders to articulate the business value of their AI component before building — prevents the common trap of 'solution looking for a problem'. (2) The cost/revenue blocks compel early thinking about unit economics and AI project ROI. (3) The stakeholder block surfaces regulatory, legal, and partnership dependencies early. (4) The one-page format is ideal for investor conversations and pitch preparation — a filled AI Project Canvas can serve as the backbone of a pitch deck's 'product' section. (5) The skills block helps founders plan team composition and identify capability gaps that might require hiring or outsourcing.
session_mapping: S3 (Projects) — directly serves the AI project scoping and management theme; the canvas is a hands-on workshop tool for students to practice framing an AI project before execution
complements: Pairs naturally with CRISP-DM (which provides the detailed project lifecycle methodology after the canvas has scoped the project's 'what' and 'why'). Also complements the ML Canvas by Louis Dorard (which goes deeper into technical ML specification: features, prediction task, evaluation — covering what the AI Project Canvas intentionally abstracts away). For teams moving toward production, the MLOps Stack Canvas picks up where the AI Project Canvas stops (deployment, monitoring, infrastructure). The AI Transformation Playbook by Andrew Ng provides the organizational context within which individual AI Project Canvases would be created for each pilot project (Step 1 of the playbook).
limitations: 1. **No technical depth**: Intentionally abstracts away ML-specific concerns like feature engineering, model architecture, evaluation methodology, and deployment pipelines — teams need supplementary frameworks (ML Canvas, MLOps Stack Canvas) for these. 2. **No GenAI/LLM coverage**: Designed for classical ML (2019), does not address foundation models, prompt engineering, RAG, fine-tuning, or generative output evaluation. 3. **No deployment or maintenance**: Stops at project scoping — does not cover model monitoring, drift detection, retraining, or operational ML concerns. 4. **No ethics or fairness block**: Unlike newer frameworks, the canvas has no dedicated space for bias assessment, fairness constraints, or regulatory compliance. 5. **Static snapshot**: Produces a one-time artifact; does not prescribe iteration, versioning, or how the canvas evolves as the project progresses. 6. **Oversimplification risk**: The 9-block format can give false confidence that a complex AI project is well-understood, when critical details (data quality, edge cases, failure modes) remain unexamined. 7. **No regulatory alignment**: Does not address EU AI Act risk classification, GDPR data requirements, or any compliance framework.
example_application:
A French fintech startup wants to build an AI-powered credit scoring system for underbanked SMEs. The team fills the AI Project Canvas in a 30-minute session:
- **Value Proposition**: 'Reduce loan default rate by 20% while expanding credit access to SMEs that traditional banks reject — creating a competitive advantage in the French SME lending market.'
- **Data**: Transaction data from partner banks (anonymized), company registration data from INSEE, publicly available financial statements, alternative data (social media, web presence).
- **Skills**: 1 ML engineer, 1 data engineer, domain expertise from a credit risk analyst, external labeling of historical loan outcomes.
- **Output**: Default probability score (AUC-ROC target > 0.85), with monthly model refresh.
- **Integration**: REST API integrated into the existing loan origination platform; decision support dashboard for credit analysts.
- **Customers**: Internal credit analysts who use the score in their decision workflow; indirectly, SME borrowers who benefit from faster, fairer decisions.
- **Stakeholders**: ACPR (French banking regulator), CNIL (data protection), legal team, partner banks providing data.
- **Cost**: 2 FTE engineers (18 months), cloud infrastructure (EUR 3K/month), data acquisition (EUR 50K), labeling (EUR 15K).
- **Revenue**: Premium pricing on AI-scored loans (higher accuracy = lower default = better margins), licensing the scoring API to other fintechs.

This one-page canvas becomes the basis for the investor pitch and the internal project kickoff.
available_templates: Free Miro templates: miro.com/miroverse/ai-canvas/ (90-120 min workshop format) and miro.com/templates/ai-product-canvas/ (AI Product Canvas variant). The original canvas image is available in the Towards Data Science article (medium.com/data-science/introducing-the-ai-project-canvas-e88e29eb7024). Syndicai provides a detailed walkthrough at syndicai.co/blog/ai-project-canvas.html. Slava Kurilyak published a document-format conversion on Medium. For the Agrawal/Gans/Goldfarb variant, templates are available via predictionmachines.ai. No official Notion template found, but the 9-block structure is easily reproducible in any tool.
regulatory_alignment: None — The AI Project Canvas (2019) predates the EU AI Act (2024), does not reference GDPR, NIST AI RMF, or ISO 42001. It has no dedicated ethics, fairness, or compliance block. Teams working in regulated industries (finance, healthcare, EU market) must supplement the canvas with regulatory-specific frameworks.
